editorial.headline: Conservation-area enterprise, read through the practical work it permits
editorial.standfirst: A conservation-area activity spanning water-based nature tourism, aquaculture infrastructure and other permanent operations, open at every business scale and to full foreign ownership nationally.
editorial.body:
KBLI 91429 concerns the management, maintenance and use of other natural-reserve areas. Its scope is operational rather than merely descriptive: the business-licensing framework covers water-based nature-tourism infrastructure; related facilities, equipment rental and services; the placement of aquaculture infrastructure; and other permanent activities in conservation areas. It is therefore a category for enterprises making an enduring, practical intervention in a conservation setting through visitor infrastructure, supporting services, fisheries-cultivation infrastructure or another fixed activity within the stated scope.

The activity is open to micro, small, medium and large businesses. That breadth means the code does not confine its underlying work to one size of operator. At the same time, its scope has a clear internal logic: it brings together stewardship functions—management and maintenance—with specified forms of use. Water-based nature tourism, associated facilities and equipment, aquaculture infrastructure, and other permanent conservation-area activities are all named as parts of that operational picture.

Nationally, foreign investment is open. The foreign-ownership ceiling is 100%, so the record sets no foreign-share cap below full ownership for this activity. The stated basis is Presidential Regulation 10/2021 and 49/2021. This is a direct national position on ownership, while the conservation-area scope gives that position its particular commercial and operational setting.

Bali does not reverse that result. The province’s island-wide, permanent moratorium blocks PMA registration for low- and medium-low-risk KBLI activities. For this activity, the Bali record states that OSS risk at the large (Besar) scale is medium-high/high; it is therefore not blocked by that moratorium, and Bali is marked as OK or higher risk. The distinction matters because Bali’s rule is broad: a national 100% ceiling does not by itself resolve every Bali question, but this record indicates no moratorium block. A foreign investor can treat the activity as open nationally and not barred from PMA registration in Bali on that moratorium ground.
